spotlight.label: Spotlight
spotlight.title: COP31 in Antalya
spotlight.intro: Bangladesh wants adaptation finance tripled and paid as grants, not loans, plus real money for loss and damage. Devlens follows what the summit means for the sector until the talks close.

today.text: Ministers are now haggling over the first draft of the summit's main decision, and the pushback is sharp. EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said the text reads like a shopping list that reopens old fights and needs significant change. Chris Bowen, who chairs the talks, expects at least one more draft before the close on Friday, 20 November. The draft's adaptation figure, at least $120 billion a year by 2035, is still far below the UNEP estimate that developing countries could need $305 billion a year by then. The second Global Stocktake was also launched in Antalya and will run until COP33. For Bangladesh, a foreign ministry side event at the Bangladesh Jute Pavilion called for predictable, grant-based finance, noting that public money for adaptation covers only about a tenth of the need, and the D-8 group, Bangladesh included, adopted an Antalya framework on climate cooperation.

watch: Adaptation finance: the draft names at least $120 billion a year by 2035. Watch whether that figure survives the next draft, expected before Friday, and whether it is counted as grants or loans.
Pushback on the draft: the EU says the text needs significant change, and Arab, Saudi and Indian objections are still open. A slimmer text could drop items developing countries want.
Just transition: the draft calls for a "just, orderly and equitable" move away from fossil fuels. Whether the Belém-Antalya Action Mechanism is adopted is still to be decided.
Electricity target: Türkiye wants electricity to cover 35% of final energy demand by 2035. Several governments have objected to putting it in the final deal.
